chunks: Where are the people who were invited to Islam and they accepted it?
They read the Qur'an and decided according to it?
They were exhorted to fight and they leapt (towards it) as she-camels leap towards their youngs.
They took their swords out of the sheaths,
and went out into the world in groups and rows?!
Some of them perished and some survived.
The good news of survival does not please them nor do they get condoled about the dead.
Their eyes have turned white with weeping.
Their bellies are emaciated because of fasting.
Their lips are dry because of (constant) praying.
Their colour is pale because of wakefulness.
Their faces bear the dust of God-fearing.
These are, my comrades who have departed. We should be justified if we feel eager for them and bite our hands in their separation!
ai.seo_question: What is Imam Ali's description of the companions' physical and spiritual state in Nahj al-Balagha?
ai.summary: In this passage from the sermon on the Battle of Siffin, Imam Ali (peace be upon him) vividly portrays the ascetic piety and physical exhaustion of the Sahaba who fought alongside him, contrasting their spiritual devotion with the political compromise of arbitration. His grief is not merely personal but reflects the loss of the ideal community that embodied the Qur'anic virtues of patience and steadfastness, a theme central to Shia historiography regarding the transition from the Rashidun era to the Umayyad caliphate. This lament underscores the concept of 'Ikhwan' (brothers) as those who shared in the struggle for divine truth, making their departure a collective tragedy for the faithful.
